# Banach Spaces on $\mathbb{R}$

## Setting Up the Problem

A Banach space is a **complete normed vector space**. To define a Banach space structure on the set $\mathbb{R}$, I need to specify:
1. A vector space structure over $\mathbb{R}$
2. A norm that makes the space complete

## Analyzing the Vector Space Structure

With the standard (and essentially unique) vector space structure, $\mathbb{R}$ is a **one-dimensional** vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ with basis $\{1\}$.

## Analyzing the Norms

Any norm $\|\cdot\|$ on a one-dimensional real vector space must satisfy:
$$\|x\| = \|x \cdot 1\| = |x| \cdot \|1\| = c|x|, \quad \text{where } c = \|1\| > 0$$

So every norm is of the form $\|x\| = c|x|$ for some $c > 0$.

## Completeness Check

For any $c > 0$, the metric $d(x,y) = c|x - y|$ is a **constant rescaling** of the standard absolute value metric. Since $(\mathbb{R}, |\cdot|)$ is complete, the space $(\mathbb{R}, c|\cdot|)$ is also complete for every $c > 0$.

Moreover, all such norms are **equivalent** (they produce the same Cauchy sequences and convergent sequences). Therefore, up to isomorphism, there is exactly **one** Banach space structure on $\mathbb{R}$.

## Conclusion

Since $\mathbb{R}$ is a one-dimensional real vector space, every possible norm makes it a complete (Banach) space, and all such norms are equivalent. There is exactly one Banach space structure on $\mathbb{R}$.

$$\boxed{1}$$
